body_markdown:
Nissan is celebrating 75 years of the Patrol nameplate by bringing it back to the United States after a decades-long hiatus. Due out for 2027, the Nissan Armada Patrol PRO-4X is an off-road-focused trim that can be decked out with several NISMO accessories.


The trim isn’t entirely new; it’s an evolution of[the existing PRO-4X model](https://www.hagerty.com/media/new-car-reviews/first-drive-2025-nissan-armada-pro-4x-is-finally-a-patrol-in-all-but-the-name/) , and it continues to offer a long list of off-road features aimed at buyers who want to leave the pavement far behind. Standard equipment includes an electronic locking rear differential (which isn’t available on any of[the other Armada trim levels](https://www.hagerty.com/media/new-car-reviews/first-drive-the-2026-armada-nismo-brings-more-power-and-exuberance-to-nissans-full-size-suv/) ), an adaptive air suspension system, and a skid plate. There’s a lot of technology packed into the SUV, including the Invisible Hood View, which provides a front-mounted wide-view camera, and eight driving modes.


Buyers who want to spend a little less time browsing aftermarket parts catalogs have three dealer-installed accessories to choose from. Nissan offers a set of Nismo Axis wheels wrapped in BF Goodrich all-terrain tires, a Nismo roof rack, and Nismo rock sliders that protect the rocker panels from expensive encounters with rocks. These parts are only offered on the Patrol PRO-4X.


Like the SL, Platinum, and Platinum Reserve trim levels, the Patrol PRO-4X is powered by a twin-turbocharged, 3.5-liter V-6 rated at 425 horsepower and 516 pound-feet of torque. Four-wheel drive and a nine-speed automatic transmission come standard.


Pricing for the 2027 Nissan Armada Patrol PRO-4X starts at $81,175, including a $2275 destination charge. For context, the base, rear-wheel-drive 2027 Armada SL carries a base price of $66,565 while the range-topping Armada Platinum Reserve 4×4 starts at $86,865. The Patrol PRO-4X will make its debut at the 2026 Los Angeles auto show, and production will start in November 2026.

## Nissan’s Land Cruiser Antidote


Nissan released the first-generation Patrol in 1951, the same year that Toyota launched the original Land Cruiser. Both landed in the burgeoning off-roader segment pioneered by[the Jeep CJ-2A](https://www.hagerty.com/media/market-trends/hagerty-insider/the-most-valuable-willys-and-jeep-cjs-from-every-generation/) . Like its rivals, the first-gen Patrol featured a relatively basic, tub-like body, a removable top, and body-on-frame construction. The second-generation Patrol, released globally in 1960, became the first Nissan-branded car sold in the United States when it arrived here in 1962; The company’s earlier cars wore Datsun emblems.


While the second-gen Patrol carried on until 1980, it retired from the American market in 1969 and wasn’t directly replaced. Sales continued in overseas markets, where the Patrol remains a popular alternative to the Toyota Land Cruiser. It sells particularly well in the Middle East and in Australia, and it’s not uncommon to spot one towing hay bales in the mountainous regions of Europe.


The nameplate is returning to our shores as a trim level for 2027, but the Patrol quietly came back over a decade ago. The second-generation Infiniti QX56 released for 2011 and the second-generation Armada introduced for 2017 were both closely related to the sixth-generation Patrol (called Y62 internally).[Infiniti’s QX80](https://www.hagerty.com/media/new-car-reviews/2026-infiniti-qx80-sport-4wd-1500-miles-in-a-not-escalade/) and the current Armada are based on the latest, Y63-gen Patrol.
